proposed.ja: パーヴェル・ドゥーロフ

terms.gloss: A playful plural coinage meaning 'mini-Durovs' — a future generation of young tech billionaires modeled on him
terms.why_hard: The Russian uses a declined plural of the surname with a prefix; a literal 'mini-Durovs' works but the tone of ironic grandiosity must be preserved

proposed.ja: ミニ・ドゥーロフたち

terms.gloss: 'Digital elite' — a journalistic label for the small class of internet entrepreneurs who achieved outsized wealth and influence
terms.why_hard: The scare quotes in the original signal ironic distance; dropping them or over-translating loses the author's register

terms.gloss: Afisha, a major Moscow lifestyle and culture magazine (1999–2015) that shaped urban hipster discourse
terms.why_hard: Unknown outside Russia; a translator must decide whether to gloss it inline or trust the reader, and this decision must be consistent every time it appears

terms.gloss: 'Think global, act local' — a well-known startup/business slogan
terms.why_hard: It is a deliberate cliché used earnestly here; a translator who doesn't recognize it as a set phrase might produce an awkward literal rendering

proposed.ja: グローバルに考え、ローカルに動く

terms.gloss: Allusion to Lermontov's 1840 novel A Hero of Our Time; capitalized here to signal the literary echo
terms.why_hard: The capitalization is the clue; a translator who misses the allusion will render it as a generic phrase and lose the ironic layer

terms.term: Как Все В Мире Будет Устроено
terms.gloss: A mock-title in capitals: 'How Everything in the World Will Be Arranged' — sarcastic reference to grand futurist manifestos
terms.why_hard: The capitalization signals a parodic book title; the translator must reproduce the mock-grandeur without adding a footnote

proposed.en: How Everything in the World Will Work

terms.gloss: 'Far-Reaching Conclusions' — another mock-capitalized phrase mocking overblown takeaways
terms.why_hard: Same device as above; must be rendered with the same mock-title treatment for consistency within the paragraph and across the book

terms.gloss: Nikolai Kononov, the author of this very book (Код Дурова)
terms.why_hard: The text refers to the author in the third person; a translator must use a consistent rendering of his name and not confuse him with Durov

terms.gloss: 'Dragged into his nets' — a predatory/fishing metaphor for acquiring users, playing on the word 'сеть' (net/network)
terms.why_hard: The pun on 'сети' (nets = networks) is central to the image; a flat translation like 'attracted users' kills the metaphor

proposed.ja: 自らの網に引き込んだ

terms.gloss: 'Stirs the imagination' — a set journalistic phrase meaning something is tantalizing or provocative
terms.why_hard: Easy to over-translate or under-translate; needs a natural equivalent that carries the same slightly breathless journalistic tone

terms.gloss: Bolshaya Morskaya Street, a major street in central St Petersburg running toward Palace Square
terms.why_hard: A translator might transliterate without noting it is a street, or confuse it with a generic 'sea' reference

proposed.ja: ボリシャヤ・モルスカヤ通り

terms.gloss: Palace Square, the central square of St Petersburg in front of the Winter Palace
terms.why_hard: Must be rendered consistently throughout; 'Palace Square' is the established English name but a careless translator might say 'Winter Palace Square'

terms.gloss: To crash at someone's place, to stay over informally (youth/internet slang of the 2000s)
terms.why_hard: The verb 'вписаться' here means to be put up informally; a literal translation like 'signed in' or 'registered' would be nonsense

terms.gloss: The wind tunnels created by St Petersburg's arched gateways (podvorotni) in winter
terms.why_hard: 'Подворотни' are the arched passageways through buildings into courtyards, a quintessential Petersburg feature; the metaphor compares them to wind tunnels

proposed.en: the wind tunnels of the gateways
proposed.ja: アーチ門の風のトンネル

terms.gloss: Glacial moraines; the snowdrifts are compared to moraines left by a glacier crawling over the pavement
terms.why_hard: The extended metaphor must be preserved; 'moraine' is a geological term that may be unfamiliar to some readers but is the intended comparison

terms.gloss: People bundled up against the cold like 'cases' or 'wrappings'; also an allusion to Chekhov's 'The Man in a Case'
terms.why_hard: The Chekhov reference adds a layer of irony (timidity, self-enclosure) that a literal 'people in cases' misses; also recurs in [112] as 'футляров'

terms.gloss: Red sailors, i.e. revolutionary sailors who stormed the Winter Palace; the tram doors 'shoot' like them
terms.why_hard: The comparison of slamming doors to revolutionary sailors is a vivid Petersburg-specific image tying to 1917; a translator must convey the military/revolutionary connotation

terms.gloss: One of the Rostral Columns on Vasilyevsky Island, iconic St Petersburg landmarks
terms.why_hard: The Rostral Columns are a well-known landmark; the text implies the narrator and friends tried to shelter inside one, which is physically possible but unusual

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, founder of VKontakte, the subject of the book
terms.why_hard: Must be rendered consistently as 'Durov' throughout; the informal context here (among students) should not shift the name rendering

terms.gloss: Approaches to the metro station; the queues stretching back about a hundred meters
terms.why_hard: 'Подступы' means the approaches or access points, not the station itself; the image is of long queues outside in the cold

terms.gloss: A handrail on an escalator or at the metro entrance; those who didn't resist were carried along it by the crowd
terms.why_hard: The image is of a crowd so dense that passive people are swept along the handrail; a translator must convey the physical danger

terms.gloss: Tasya, a diminutive of Taisia, a girl who sat next to Durov in class and liked him
terms.why_hard: The diminutive form signals informality and youth; a translator should keep it as a familiar name rather than expanding to full form

terms.gloss: Copper coins, small change; the girl brought Durov small coins which he poured into his briefcase
terms.why_hard: 'Медяки' is colloquial for small-denomination coins; the image suggests a child's innocent generosity or perhaps a superstition

terms.gloss: Occupied the front desk (in a classroom); 'оккупировал' is humorous military metaphor for claiming a seat
terms.why_hard: 'Оккупировал' is deliberately hyperbolic and humorous; a flat translation like 'sat at' loses the tone

proposed.ja: 最前列の席を占拠した

terms.term: третья строчка снизу яснее не стала
terms.gloss: The third line from the bottom didn't become any clearer; Durov is straining to read what is written on the blackboard
terms.why_hard: This is an interior monologue fragment showing Durov's difficulty reading the board; a translator must preserve the slightly detached, observational tone

proposed.en: the third line from the bottom was no clearer
proposed.zh: 倒数第三行还是看不清
proposed.ja: 下から三行目は相変わらず読めない

terms.gloss: A tram line; St Petersburg has an extensive tram network and the characters plan to ride a long route to sleep
terms.why_hard: The tram is a deliberate choice of transport (cheap, long route, warm enough); a translator should not substitute 'bus' or generic 'public transport'

terms.gloss: The Rusakovs, a married couple of educators who ran the experimental school (классы) where Durov's father taught.
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might treat them as a one-off mention or fail to connect them to the 'энтузиасты' (enthusiasts) who ran the classes; the surname needs consistent transliteration.

terms.gloss: Literally 'the classes'; the informal name for the experimental school/study group run by the Rusakovs that Durov attended.
terms.why_hard: Could be mistaken for ordinary 'classrooms' rather than a specific proper noun referring to this particular educational collective.

terms.gloss: Diminutive of талоны (coupons/vouchers); refers to meal tickets or vouchers used in Soviet/post-Soviet canteens.
terms.why_hard: The diminutive suffix conveys a specific Soviet-era intimacy and privation that a generic 'tickets' or 'coupons' misses.

terms.gloss: The Metropol Hotel, a historic luxury hotel in Moscow (or a restaurant/café named after it).
terms.why_hard: Could be confused with a generic 'metropole' or cinema; it signifies pre-revolutionary luxury in the Russian context.

terms.gloss: Minimum wage; specifically the minimum monthly wage in Russia in the early 1990s (which was 83 rubles at that time).
terms.why_hard: Might be translated as 'minimum salary' without capturing the specific economic indicator 'minimum wage' (МРОТ) or the historical irony of the amount.

terms.gloss: Self-financing; the economic principle that an institution must cover its own costs without state subsidy.
terms.why_hard: A literal translation like 'self-payment' would obscure this specific Soviet/post-Soviet economic term meaning financial self-sufficiency.

terms.gloss: A period of ordeal and wandering; wearying peregrinations from one difficult place to another.
terms.why_hard: Weтарства is a culturally specific word (originally referring to the ordeal of souls after death) that conveys prolonged bureaucratic or physical wandering with hardship; 'travels' or 'wanderings' is too neutral.

terms.gloss: Professor Durov, Pavel Durov's father (Valery Durov), a doctor of philological sciences.
terms.why_hard: The title 'профессор' is an academic rank; inconsistent rendering (sometimes 'Professor', sometimes just 'Dr.') would confuse the reader about his status.

terms.gloss: The haughty/arrogant younger son; refers to Pavel Durov himself as a boy.
terms.why_hard: Заносчивый is a specific character judgment (aloof, stuck-up) that defines Durov's early portrayal; softening it to 'proud' or 'confident' loses the edge.

terms.gloss: Problems/tests designed to assess linguistic intuition or aptitude for languages.
terms.why_hard: Чутье (flair/intuition) might be rendered as 'feeling' or 'sense', but 'linguistic intuition' is the standard term in language testing.

proposed.ja: 言語的直感を問う課題

terms.gloss: A non-existent/constructed language; a made-up language used for the linguistics test.
terms.why_hard: Could be mistranslated as 'a language that doesn't exist' without conveying that this was an artificial/constructed language specifically designed for the test.

terms.gloss: Scanty/meager introductory data; the minimal given information provided for solving the linguistics puzzle.
terms.why_hard: Вводные here means 'input data' or 'given information', not 'introductions'; it is a specific term in problem-solving contexts.

terms.gloss: Grigory Mednikov, the new director of the experimental school.
terms.why_hard: Proper name requiring consistent transliteration; the patronymic and surname must be rendered consistently across the book.

proposed.ja: グリゴリー・メドニコフ

terms.gloss: A constructivist-style House of Culture (community center/club).
terms.why_hard: Constructivism is a specific Soviet architectural style of the 1920s-30s; 'constructivist' must be preserved to convey the architectural/historical period.

proposed.zh: 构成主义风格的文化宫
proposed.ja: 構成主義様式の文化会館

terms.gloss: Narvskaya, a Saint Petersburg Metro station (on the Kirovsko-Vyborgskaya Line).
terms.why_hard: Must be identified as a metro station name; inconsistent transliteration (Narvskaya vs. Narvskaia) or failure to identify it as a station would confuse geography.

terms.gloss: Poetry tournaments; public poetry competitions/recitations popular in the 1960s Soviet cultural scene.
terms.why_hard: The specific format of 1960s Soviet 'poetry tournaments' (improvised verse competitions) might be flattened into generic 'poetry readings'.

terms.gloss: Joseph Brodsky, the Nobel Prize-winning Russian poet (1940-1996).
terms.why_hard: Must be recognized as the famous poet; the reference signals the cultural prestige of the venue.

terms.gloss: Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) club/chapter.
terms.why_hard: The standard name is 'Alcoholics Anonymous'; rendering it as 'club of anonymous alcoholics' preserves the word order but loses the institutional recognition.

proposed.ja: アルコホーリクス・アノニマス

terms.gloss: Seventh-day Adventists; members of the Protestant Christian denomination.
terms.why_hard: Could be confused with 'adventurers'; refers specifically to the religious denomination known for Saturday worship and health practices.

proposed.zh: 基督复临安息日会信徒

terms.gloss: The Dancing Pensioner, a club/café for elderly people (pensioners).
terms.why_hard: The ironic name (dancing + pensioner) might be translated too literally or lose the specific Russian cultural reference to state-run leisure clubs for retirees.

terms.gloss: Action-packed circumstances; highly dramatic/thrilling surroundings (ironic reference to the eclectic mix of organizations in the building).
terms.why_hard: Остросюжетный (literally 'sharp-plotted') is an ironic literary term usually applied to thrillers/detective stories; applying it to physical circumstances is a specific narrative joke.

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, co-founder of VKontakte and the biography's protagonist
terms.why_hard: Declined form only; the book's central name must be transliterated identically across all segments and languages

terms.gloss: VKontakte, the Russian social network founded by Durov
terms.why_hard: Whether to keep the Cyrillic-brand form, transliterate, or use the later 'VK' must be decided once

terms.gloss: The 1999 TV film 'Pirates of Silicon Valley' about Jobs and Gates
terms.why_hard: Russian title differs from the original; translator must map back to the known English film title rather than translate literally

proposed.ja: 『パイレーツ・オブ・シリコンバレー』

terms.gloss: Steve Jobs
terms.why_hard: Standard but must match the established transliteration of his name in each target language

terms.gloss: 'homunculus identities' — fake/secondary online personae as artificial little humans
terms.why_hard: The alchemical 'homunculus' allusion (artificially created miniature human) can be lost if rendered as plain 'fake identities'

proposed.ja: ホムンクルス的アイデンティティ

terms.gloss: 'a potent salesman of ideas' — Durov as charismatic persuader, echoing 'reality distortion field'
terms.why_hard: 'сильнодействующий' is drug-medicine register ('powerful-acting'); flattening it to 'persuasive' loses the narcotic flavor

proposed.zh: 一位极具效力的理念推销员
proposed.ja: 強烈な「アイデアのセールスマン」

terms.term: so long, and thanks for all the fish
terms.gloss: English quotation kept in English in the Russian text, title of Douglas Adams's fourth Hitchhiker's book
terms.why_hard: It is already English embedded in Russian; the translator must decide whether to keep the code-switching effect or translate

proposed.en: so long, and thanks for all the fish
proposed.ja: さようなら、そして魚をありがとう

terms.gloss: Official Russian title of Adams's novel, given in the footnote
terms.why_hard: The footnote title should match the established published translation title in each language

proposed.en: So Long, and Thanks for All the Fish
proposed.ja: 『さようなら、そして魚をありがとう』

terms.gloss: Douglas Adams, British comic SF author
terms.why_hard: Standard, but transliteration must be the established one in each language

terms.gloss: 'The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy' series title in Russian
terms.why_hard: Russian series title uses singular 'galaxy' and omits 'guide'; must map to each language's established translation title

proposed.en: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy
proposed.ja: 『銀河ヒッチハイク・ガイド』

terms.gloss: Vogons, the bureaucratic alien race in Adams's series
terms.why_hard: Transliteration of 'Vogon' differs by language; must use each language's canonical Adams translation

terms.gloss: hyperspace bypass/express route — the Vogons' reason for demolishing Earth
terms.why_hard: Adams's phrase 'hyperspatial express route/bypass' should match the canonical translation, not an ad-hoc rendering

terms.gloss: Chapter 1 heading
terms.why_hard: Trivial but must be uniform in formatting across all chapters and languages

terms.gloss: 'Botanical Garden' — chapter title and the St Petersburg district near the Botanical Garden / Botanicheskaya street where Durov grew up
terms.why_hard: It's both a literal garden and a neighborhood reference; capitalizing it as a proper place name vs. a generic garden is a real decision

terms.gloss: a volume of Cervantes — signals the boy's bookishness; Don Quixote implied
terms.why_hard: Translator may want to specify Don Quixote, but the Russian deliberately says just 'a tome of Cervantes'; over-specifying changes the texture

terms.gloss: the entrance/stairwell of a Soviet-style apartment block
terms.why_hard: No direct equivalent in English/Japanese; 'entrance hall', 'stairwell', or 'front door' change the Soviet housing connotation

proposed.en: the entrance of his apartment block
proposed.ja: アパートのエントランス

terms.gloss: 'some scoundrel' — mock-indignant register for the inconsiderate parker
terms.why_hard: The old-fashioned, slightly comic indignation tone can be lost if rendered as neutral 'someone'

terms.gloss: high-voltage transmission towers (pylons)
terms.why_hard: 'вышка' is 'tower', not 'pylon'; consistent term needed for the industrial landscape motif

terms.gloss: Saint Petersburg
terms.why_hard: Colloquial short form; must decide whether to use 'St Petersburg', 'Petersburg', or 彼得堡-style colloquial forms consistently

terms.gloss: slightly ironic colloquialism for 'face'
terms.why_hard: Register marker; 'face' is flat, 'mug' too slangy — the ironic bookish-casual tone must be hit

terms.gloss: 'as they say' — discourse marker framing the Adams quote
terms.why_hard: Trivial but recurs; must be rendered with a consistent tag across the book

terms.gloss: 'the hero' — the author's ironic-epic label for Durov as his book's protagonist
terms.why_hard: Recurring epithet: 'hero' vs 'protagonist' vs 'subject' must be fixed once, as it carries the book's mock-epic tone

terms.gloss: 'the author' — first-person narrator referring to himself in third person
terms.why_hard: The narrator alternates 'I' and 'the author'; keeping or smoothing this self-distance is a book-wide voice decision

terms.term: систему каналов, в которых бежит чужая жизнь
terms.gloss: 'a system of channels in which other people's lives flow' — VKontakte figured as canals carrying life
terms.why_hard: Canal metaphor alludes to St Petersburg's canals; reading it as mere 'communication channels' loses the city image

proposed.en: a system of channels carrying other people's lives
proposed.zh: 一套流淌着他人生活的运河系统
proposed.ja: 他人の人生が流れる運河のシステム

terms.gloss: 'the sea is nearby' — the Gulf of Finland near the Botanicheskaya district
terms.why_hard: Reader without geography may miss that this pins the district; deciding whether to name the gulf is a judgment call

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, co-founder and CEO of VKontakte, referred to by first name
terms.why_hard: Russian first-name familiarity must stay consistent as Pavel, not Paul or Pasha

terms.gloss: the foreign business executive negotiating with Durov, repeatedly labelled only as 'the expat'
terms.why_hard: the Russian word carries an ironic, slightly sneering status sense that neutral 'foreigner' loses

terms.gloss: Ilya Perekopsky, then VKontakte vice-president, one of Durov's inner circle
terms.why_hard: missing surname means the translator must identify the correct Ilya from VK history

terms.gloss: Andrey, likely a senior VK technical colleague in Durov's team; exact identity needs pinning
terms.why_hard: first name alone; the book assumes a Russian reader knows which Andrey

terms.gloss: a Swiss chalet offered as a private, neutral, luxurious venue for off-site talks
terms.why_hard: carries a signal of wealth and informal deal-making; rendering it as just 'house' loses that

terms.gloss: the negotiator of the trio, one of Durov's two companions running the deal talk
terms.why_hard: a recurring role label; if translated differently each time, the running cast becomes unclear

terms.gloss: capitalized recurring epithet for the programmer among Durov's companions
terms.why_hard: Russian uses the role like a nickname; English needs a consistent definite 'the programmer'

terms.gloss: running comic epithet for Durov as leader of a 'gang'
terms.why_hard: the criminal-gang humour must not read as factual organized crime

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, referred to by surname here
terms.why_hard: transliteration must remain consistent with first-name references and with real-world usage

terms.gloss: Durov's sarcastic accusation that the expat is acting like a bribe-giving corrupt official
terms.why_hard: Russian коррупционер usually denotes an official who takes bribes; the jab needs that charge to land

terms.gloss: a Soviet-era ministry that survived into the present, evoked by its dated gilded lift
terms.why_hard: the joke depends on knowing the shabby-grand Soviet bureaucratic aesthetic

proposed.en: a relic of a Soviet ministry
proposed.zh: 前苏联时代遗存下来的部委
proposed.ja: ソ連時代の遺物のような官庁

terms.gloss: a sequence of offices with doors aligned, in the classical grand-palace layout
terms.why_hard: architectural term unusual for a modern office; conveys pomp and incongruity

proposed.zh: 成排相连、房门贯通的办公室

terms.gloss: the trio of Durov, Ilya and Andrey, labelled as a capitalized 'Trinity/Trio'
terms.why_hard: capitalized label with possible Holy Trinity irony; must stay a running term

terms.gloss: the foreigner's face frozen in shock, as if turned to stone
terms.why_hard: literal 'petrified' can sound archaeological or comic in the wrong register

proposed.ja: 凍りついた外国人の顔

terms.term: магнитные доски, где литерами были набраны таблички
terms.gloss: magnetic notice boards whose signs are spelled out with movable individual letters
terms.why_hard: not ordinary printed signs; the letter-by-letter detail adds to the shabby office humour

proposed.en: magnetic boards whose signs were set in individual letters
proposed.zh: 用单个字母拼贴出来的磁性标牌
proposed.ja: 活字のように文字を並べた磁石ボード

terms.gloss: joke internal VK team/room sign: 'Squat IE' and 'Bones in the Tank'; likely obscure insider names
terms.why_hard: probably an in-joke even to many Russians; the sign must survive as a sign, not be normalised

proposed.ja: 「IEのスクワット。戦車の中の骨」

terms.gloss: Soviet People's Commissariat for Enlightenment (1917–46); used here as a jokey team name
terms.why_hard: historical Soviet acronym with zero resonance abroad unless glossed or rendered as a period piece

proposed.en: Narkompros, the People's Commissariat for Enlightenment
proposed.ja: 人民啓蒙委員部（ナルコムプロス）

terms.gloss: probably an internal VK team handling abusive or difficult users
terms.why_hard: reads like an official team name, not a random description; consistency matters

terms.gloss: self-mocking office sign 'Durov Museum' among the VK rooms
terms.why_hard: the joke is personal-cult irony; losing 'museum' loses the gag

terms.gloss: geek/startup anti-style detail: T-shirts cinched by belts above the waist
terms.why_hard: describes a specific nerd-fashion gesture that signals the office culture

proposed.en: T-shirts cinched with belts above the waist
proposed.zh: 用皮带把T恤束在腰间的穿法
proposed.ja: 腰上でベルトを締め付けたTシャツ

terms.gloss: shirts buttoned up to the very top, a deliberately prim nerd style statement
terms.why_hard: reads as an intentional stylistic quirk, not an ordinary description of clothing

proposed.en: shirts proudly buttoned to the top button
proposed.zh: 把衬衫扣到最上面一颗扣子
proposed.ja: 一番上のボタンまできっちり留めたシャツ

terms.gloss: Surname of a family of philologists, friends of Durov's father
terms.why_hard: Must be transliterated consistently and styled as a family name

terms.gloss: Academic Gymnasium of St. Petersburg State University, a prestigious secondary school
terms.why_hard: The official name and its rendering in target languages need verification

proposed.en: St. Petersburg State University Academic Gymnasium
proposed.zh: 圣彼得堡国立大学附属文科中学
proposed.ja: サンクトペテルブルク大学付属ギムナジウム

terms.gloss: The period of uncontrolled freedom in education after the Soviet collapse
terms.why_hard: The phrase 'вольница' evokes historical free Cossack communities; a literal translation loses the connotation of chaotic liberty

proposed.ja: 教育における自由放任

terms.gloss: Embezzlement or illegal skimming of budget funds ('sawing' the money)
terms.why_hard: The slang term 'пилить' (to saw) for misappropriating funds is specific to Russian bureaucratic jargon

terms.gloss: Ethnic Germans who were resettled (often forcibly) to Siberia, such as the Volga Germans
terms.why_hard: The term may imply forced deportation; a careless translation as 'German settlers' erases the Soviet history

terms.gloss: The Soviet name of St. Petersburg, used here for the period before 1991
terms.why_hard: The city's name changed; consistency with 'Петербург' elsewhere in the text is essential

terms.gloss: St. Petersburg, referred to informally without 'Санкт-'
terms.why_hard: The informal Russian name must be rendered appropriately to match the register

proposed.ja: サンクトペテルブルク

terms.gloss: Short for журналистский факультет (journalism faculty/department)
terms.why_hard: The abbreviation is informal; a formal equivalent might sound unnatural

terms.gloss: Cradle of the intelligentsia, referring to St. Petersburg as the birthplace of Russian intellectual culture
terms.why_hard: The term 'intelligentsia' carries specific cultural weight; the metaphor should not be flattened

proposed.ja: インテリゲンチャの揺籃

terms.gloss: Anichkov Palace on Nevsky Prospekt, a historic building in St. Petersburg
terms.why_hard: The name and location are well-known; mistransliteration would confuse readers

proposed.zh: 涅瓦大街上的阿尼奇科夫宫
proposed.ja: ネフスキー大通りのアニチコフ宮殿

terms.gloss: Julius Caesar's Commentaries on the Gallic War, a standard Latin text
terms.why_hard: The title has established translations in each language; using a non-standard version would be jarring

terms.gloss: The Russian Ministry of Education
terms.why_hard: The ministry's name changed over time; the translator should use the appropriate historical name

terms.gloss: The Singer House, an Art Nouveau building on Nevsky Prospekt that housed VKontakte's headquarters and is a St Petersburg landmark.
terms.why_hard: A careless translator might render it as 'Singer House' without signaling it is a famous building, or might transliterate it oddly; it also recurs as a metonym for the company throughout the book.

terms.gloss: VKontakte, Russia's dominant social network, often called 'Russian Facebook' in Western media.
terms.why_hard: Translators must decide once whether to use 'VKontakte', 'VK', or leave it in Cyrillic; inconsistency across the book would confuse readers.

terms.gloss: The bronze Valkyrie sculptures on the Singer Building's façade, a decorative element of the building.
terms.why_hard: A translator unfamiliar with the building might render 'Valkyries' without noting they are sculptural figures on the roof, losing the visual image of silent sentinels overlooking the street.

terms.gloss: A Russian transliteration of English 'nerds', used here to describe the tech-savvy generation that reshaped the world.
terms.why_hard: The term is deliberately borrowed from English; a translator must decide whether to keep the foreign flavor or use a native equivalent, and this choice must be consistent with how the word appears elsewhere in the book.

terms.gloss: Literally 'broke the picture of the world', meaning shattered or overturned the prevailing worldview.
terms.why_hard: A literal translation ('broke the picture of the world') sounds unnatural in English; the idiom needs a natural equivalent that preserves the sense of a paradigm shift.

terms.gloss: A 'construction set made of high-rises', describing the repetitive, modular appearance of Soviet-era apartment blocks seen from above or in rows.
terms.why_hard: The image evokes the monotonous Soviet housing estates; a translator who doesn't catch this cultural context might render it as a generic 'row of tall buildings' and lose the critical, slightly ironic tone.

proposed.en: a construction set of tower blocks
proposed.ja: 高層住宅のコンストラクター

terms.gloss: Crowding or jostling, here referring to the push and shove at a handrail or grab-pole in public transport.
terms.why_hard: Very colloquial and physical; needs a word that conveys the compressed, unpleasant bodily experience of rush-hour transit.

terms.gloss: Cursing at cars merging from the right — a reference to Russian road etiquette and the irritation of drivers being cut off.
terms.why_hard: The phrase is very specific to Russian driving culture; a translator needs to convey the universal frustration while keeping the specificity of the traffic context.

proposed.en: cursing at those merging from the right
proposed.zh: 对右侧强行并线车辆的咒骂
proposed.ja: 右から割り込む車への悪口

terms.gloss: The St Petersburg Metro, which is notably deep and ornate.
terms.why_hard: In this context it is part of a sequence describing a typical morning commute; the translator should keep it simple but not lose the sense that this is a specific urban routine.

terms.gloss: A slightly old-fashioned or diminutive word for photographs, here used to describe the small images people share on social media.
terms.why_hard: The word carries a slightly archaic, almost tender tone contrasted with modern technology; a translator should find an equivalent that hints at this slight anachronism or intimacy.

terms.gloss: Likely Kazan Cathedral, which is directly across the Nevsky from the Singer Building.
terms.why_hard: The text does not name the cathedral; a translator might leave it generic ('the cathedral') or add a clarifying note. The choice affects whether the scene feels anchored in a specific place.

terms.gloss: The 'war' refers to the ongoing corporate and legal conflicts surrounding VKontakte from its earliest days.
terms.why_hard: The word is used metaphorically throughout the book; a translator must decide whether to keep 'war' or soften it to 'conflict' or 'battle', and this must be consistent across all segments.

terms.gloss: A voice recorder or dictaphone, used here to record a negotiation meeting.
terms.why_hard: The word 'dictaphone' in English can sound dated; the translator should decide whether to use 'voice recorder' or keep 'dictaphone' for a slightly old-fashioned feel.

terms.gloss: The person on the other end of a phone or video call; a standard telecom term in Russian.
terms.why_hard: In English 'subscriber' is the literal equivalent but sounds technical; 'the person on the other end' or 'the caller' would be more natural but less precise.

proposed.en: the person on the other end

terms.gloss: Literally 'buried in newspapers', a common Russian expression for people absorbed in reading.
terms.why_hard: The verb уткнуться means to bury one's face into something; a translator should find a natural equivalent that conveys the same physical absorption without being awkward.

terms.gloss: The medium or carrier of information, here contrasting newspapers with phones.
terms.why_hard: The word is abstract and technical; in English 'medium' works well but the translator must ensure it doesn't sound too academic for the reflective, essayistic tone of the passage.

terms.gloss: Consciousness and psyche — a pair that in Russian covers both intellectual awareness and deeper psychological makeup.
terms.why_hard: In English 'consciousness and psyche' can sound clinical; the translator needs to find a pair that sounds natural in a literary-essayistic context without losing the breadth of meaning.

terms.gloss: The bridges of St Petersburg, famously raised at night during navigation season.
terms.why_hard: The mention of bridges in the context of night is a subtle nod to the raising of St Petersburg's bridges; a translator who doesn't catch this might miss the atmospheric significance.

terms.gloss: Literally 'plunged into night', describing the city falling into darkness.
terms.why_hard: The phrase is poetic and atmospheric; a translator should preserve the literary quality without making it sound overwrought in the target language.

terms.gloss: Multi-storey apartment buildings, specifically the mass-produced Soviet-era housing blocks (Khrushchyovkas or Brezhnevkas) that dominate Russian residential areas.
terms.why_hard: The word evokes a very specific type of Soviet housing; a translator who renders it simply as 'high-rises' loses the cultural connotation of uniformity and mass production.

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, founder of VKontakte, subject of the biography
terms.why_hard: Full name vs surname-only must match the book's established convention in each language

terms.gloss: A classmate/interviewee whose recollections the author reports
terms.why_hard: A minor real person; needs consistent transliteration and an early signal that he is a source, not an actor

terms.gloss: To lecture in a preachy, mentor-like tone (said ironically of Durov)
terms.why_hard: Irony must survive; 'mentor' as a verb is awkward in all three targets

terms.gloss: Theatrical/literary type: a character who moralizes at length; here Durov's classroom persona
terms.why_hard: No everyday equivalent; literal 'reasoner' reads oddly, though the word recurs in Russian criticism

terms.gloss: First half of the proverb 'работа не волк, в лес не убежит' — work won't run away, i.e. it can wait
terms.why_hard: Truncated quotation assumes the reader knows the full proverb; must supply or evoke it in en/ja

proposed.en: 'work isn't a wolf — it won't run off into the woods'
proposed.zh: “活儿不是狼，不会跑进树林里”
proposed.ja: 「仕事は狼じゃない、森へ逃げたりしない」

terms.gloss: Ivan Goncharov, 19th-c. Russian novelist, author of Oblomov
terms.why_hard: Bare surname; readers may not know him, but adding 'the novelist' must be done consistently for all classic authors here

terms.gloss: The famously idle gentry hero of Goncharov's novel; archetype of laziness in Russian culture
terms.why_hard: Core allusion of the paragraph; 'milыi Oblomov' (endearing) is the author's slighting spin, easily lost

proposed.zh: 惹人怜爱的奥勃洛莫夫
proposed.ja: 愛すべきオブローモフ

terms.gloss: Andrei Stolz, the energetic German-Russian counter-hero of Oblomov
terms.why_hard: 'Mechanistic Stolz' compresses a long literary debate; Durov's pejorative framing must carry over

terms.gloss: Fyodor Dostoevsky, the novelist
terms.why_hard: Universally known, but the reported claim 'terrible writer' is provocative; tone, not knowledge, is the risk

terms.gloss: Chekhov's last play, whose plot the class argues over
terms.why_hard: Chekhov is unnamed; the play's title itself must signal the whole debate to readers

terms.gloss: The merchant in The Cherry Orchard who buys and fells the estate's orchard
terms.why_hard: 'Man of action' is Durov's approving gloss, against the standard sentimental reading; contrast must land

terms.gloss: Lyubov Ranevskaya, the feckless landowner of The Cherry Orchard
terms.why_hard: Only appears inside a metaphor; her identity and the booted-into-lace-soul image depend on knowing the play

terms.gloss: Set phrase from a popular aphorism about the merchant class trampling refined culture 'in its boots'
terms.why_hard: A famous Russian quip; the tactile boots/lace antithesis should be preserved, not paraphrased away

proposed.en: bursting in its boots into Ranevskaya's lace-fringed soul
proposed.zh: 穿着靴子踩进朗涅夫斯卡娅蕾丝般娇弱的灵魂
proposed.ja: 長靴のままラネーフスカヤのレースのような魂に踏み込む

terms.gloss: 'Our wondrous country' — ironic stock phrase for Russia
terms.why_hard: Irony ('marvelous' as sarcastic) must be kept; literal 'wonderful' reads sincere in en/zh/ja

terms.gloss: Slang: to mouth off against everyone, to trash everything indiscriminately
terms.why_hard: Register — teenage street slang of the 2000s reported in retrospect; needs casual equivalents, not neutral 'criticize'

proposed.ja: やたらにケチをつける

terms.gloss: The class nearly came to blows over the argument
terms.why_hard: Colloquial 'передраться' implies near-fight; understating loses the comic heat

proposed.ja: ほとんど殴り合い寸前になった

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, founder of VKontakte
terms.why_hard: surname transliteration must stay consistent across the book

terms.gloss: VKontakte, the social network Durov founded
terms.why_hard: must choose one brand rendering and not confuse it with the later VK rebrand

terms.gloss: US electronic stock exchange
terms.why_hard: proper exchange name; evokes a billion-dollar publicly traded tech company

terms.gloss: allusion to Durov's father being a philology professor
terms.why_hard: careless translator may flatten it to 'professor's son' and lose the intellectual-elite coding

terms.gloss: VK described as a digital state
terms.why_hard: recurring nation-state metaphor for VK must stay consistent

terms.gloss: a trick or feint pulled off right under the state's nose
terms.why_hard: Russian idiom combines a sports feint with spatial defiance; needs idiomatic equivalent, not literal movement

proposed.en: a trick pulled under the state's nose
proposed.zh: 在国家眼皮底下玩了个花招
proposed.ja: 国家の鼻先でやってのけたトリック

terms.gloss: era of petty themes, small-minded fear among businessmen
terms.why_hard: obscure coined period word with political timidity connotations; literal rendering loses it

proposed.zh: 人人自危、话题收缩的时代

terms.gloss: Putin-era 'power vertical', centralized chain of command
terms.why_hard: political term of art; translator must decide between calque and explanatory equivalent

terms.gloss: Russian internet-industry news site
terms.why_hard: proper name should be kept, but target readers may need implicit sense of a trade outlet

terms.gloss: unauthorized or pirated films, in scare quotes
terms.why_hard: quotation marks signal contested, colloquial usage; must preserve ironic distance

terms.gloss: mounted or caught and rode the trend
terms.why_hard: riding metaphor should stay idiomatic, not become literal horse-riding

proposed.ja: トレンドを乗りこなした

terms.gloss: rakes in cash or dough, vulgar register
terms.why_hard: register is deliberately low and quoted from a comment; polishing it would misrepresent the voice

terms.gloss: Twitter nickname mentioned in the text; identity requires checking
terms.why_hard: English alias with loaded 'porn' meaning; must decide whether to preserve, translate, or gloss

terms.gloss: quoted description of the platform as a new nervous system
terms.why_hard: quoted phrase likely linked to earlier tech discourse; must preserve biological-network metaphor

terms.gloss: VK as a state of nerds
terms.why_hard: recurring VK state metaphor plus nerd/geek cultural term; zh and ja need natural nerd word

terms.gloss: Alexander Bek, Tom Wolfe, Truman Capote, writers associated with striking narrative nonfiction
terms.why_hard: Russian genitive forms must be reconstructed and transliterated separately in each target language

proposed.ja: ベック、ウルフ、カポーティ

terms.gloss: hunters for outstanding true stories, New Journalism ideal
terms.why_hard: hunting metaphor defines their ethos; a flat 'reporters' loses the point

proposed.zh: 追逐杰出真实故事的猎手
proposed.ja: 優れた実話を追うハンターたち

terms.gloss: The VK-side negotiator in the scene, one of Durov's team members; epithet used as his only name.
terms.why_hard: A recurring label, not a name; must stay consistent and not drift into 'the talks-man' or 'the interlocutor'.

terms.gloss: Slightly ironic Russian slang for a foreign (Western) business expatriate working in Russia.
terms.why_hard: Not just 'expat' — carries condescending, period-marked irony; 'the foreigner' later refers to the same man and must align.

proposed.ja: エクスパット（外資系駐在員）

terms.gloss: Same foreign visitor as 'экспат', referred to by a different epithet in [23].
terms.why_hard: Translator must recognize this is the same character, or the reader thinks a new person entered.

proposed.zh: 外国人（即前文的外方经理）

terms.gloss: Yet a third epithet for the same expat in [22] — 'the manager said firmly'.
terms.why_hard: Three labels for one person in six paragraphs; consistency mapping is essential.

terms.gloss: A VK programmer present at the meeting, silently coding through the negotiation.
terms.why_hard: His deadpan presence is a joke; must stay 'the programmer', not become a generic 'engineer'.

terms.gloss: The eccentric figure (strongly implied to be Durov himself) who shouts and storms around; 'тип' is dismissive slang.
terms.why_hard: 'Тип' = 'character/guy' with irony; and the hint that this is Durov must survive — later chapters will confirm identity.

proposed.en: the guy in the baseball cap

terms.gloss: VK's 'Wishes/Gifts' service letting users buy virtual gifts for friends in VK's internal currency (votes).
terms.why_hard: Product name; a real VK feature ('Мои желания'/gifts) — needs correct official or descriptive rendering used consistently.

terms.gloss: VK's internal virtual currency — 'votes' (голоса), purchasable with real money.
terms.why_hard: 'Our currency' is a pointed in-world phrase; translator should keep the opacity or add the well-known term 'votes'.

proposed.zh: 我们的虚拟货币（VK投票币）

terms.gloss: The one-click buy button VK offers the vendor — the standard e-commerce '1-click' pitch.
terms.why_hard: Echoes Amazon's 'one-click' trope; rendering must keep the sales-pitch register.

proposed.en: a button that lets a customer buy a gift with one click
proposed.ja: ワンクリックでギフトを購入できるボタン

terms.gloss: Inventory turnover — how fast a product category sells; standard retail metric.
terms.why_hard: Business jargon; a careless translator would render it as 'rotation' or vaguely as 'popularity'.

terms.gloss: The cliché 'it's just business, nothing personal'.
terms.why_hard: Fixed English idiom in origin; must be rendered by the equivalent cliché, not paraphrased.

proposed.ja: ビジネスです、個人的な話ではありません

terms.gloss: 'Reinforced-concrete' — Russian slang for an unshakeable, cast-iron conviction.
terms.why_hard: Distinctive period slang; literal translation is comic nonsense, but the deadpan hardness of the metaphor is worth keeping.

proposed.en: had learned it, cast in concrete,
proposed.ja: 鉄の信念として叩き込んでいた

terms.term: Всему есть цена, и благородные устремления существуют, чтобы набить цену
terms.gloss: Cynical maxim: everything has a price, and noble aspirations exist only to drive the price up ('набить цену' = to inflate one's asking price by posing).
terms.why_hard: 'Набить цену' is a haggling idiom (to posture/hold out for more), often mistranslated as simply 'raise the price'.

proposed.en: everything has a price, and noble aspirations exist only to drive the price up
proposed.zh: 万物皆有价，而高尚的追求不过是抬价用的
proposed.ja: すべてには値段がつく。崇高な理想とは、値段を釣り上げるためだけに存在する

terms.gloss: 'The guys are just haggling' — the expat's dismissive read of VK's posturing.
terms.why_hard: Ties into the haggling motif; 'торгуются' is market-stall haggling, not formal 'negotiating' — register matters.

proposed.zh: 这帮家伙不过是在讨价还价。
proposed.ja: 連中はただ値切りしているだけだ。

terms.gloss: Soft/plush toys — one of the vendor's gift categories in the VK gift shop.
terms.why_hard: Mundane but recurring product category in the commission split; keep literal and consistent.

terms.gloss: The commission percentage VK demands, escalating from 10 to 20 as absurd pressure.
terms.why_hard: Numeric escalation is the scene's joke; percent vs percentage-point phrasing must not wobble.

terms.term: Покрутил головой и продолжил стучать по клавиатуре
terms.gloss: The programmer shakes his head slightly and keeps typing through the shouting — deadpan counterpoint.
terms.why_hard: 'Покрутил головой' is ambiguous (shake/turn); the comic timing of his indifference must survive.

proposed.en: gave a small shake of his head and kept hammering at his keyboard
proposed.ja: 首を少し振ると、キーを叩き続けた

terms.gloss: Russian gesture-idiom: spread his hands in a shrug of 'what can you do'.
terms.why_hard: Gesture idiom; literal 'spread his arms' misreads as stretching; it's a shrug of finality.

proposed.en: spread his hands in a shrug
proposed.ja: 両手を広げて肩をすくめた

terms.gloss: Suddenly bellowed — the tonal whiplash of the 20-percent ultimatum.
terms.why_hard: 'Заорал' is louder and cruder than 'said loudly'; the absurd escalation depends on verb force.

terms.term: Сунул руки в карманы черных брюк
terms.gloss: Hands thrust into the pockets of black trousers — Durov's signature all-black outfit detail.
terms.why_hard: This is a recognizable Durov visual motif recurring across the book; keep the black clothes detail intact.

proposed.en: thrust his hands into the pockets of his black trousers
proposed.ja: 黒いズボンのポケットに手を突っ込んだ

terms.gloss: Walking slightly lopsided, leaning forward — Durov's distinctive gait/stance in this scene.
terms.why_hard: Rare descriptive verb 'скособочившись'; clumsiness would blur the recognizable physical portrait.

proposed.ja: 少し体を傾け、前かがみになりながら

terms.gloss: 'Деятель' — dismissive/ironic Russian word for an operator or 'character' in public life.
terms.why_hard: 'Деятель' is loaded irony (a self-important busybody); 'person' or 'figure' loses the sarcasm.

terms.gloss: Free indirect thought of the expat: 'we're all respectable people here' — corporate-Western reflex colliding with the theater he's watching.
terms.why_hard: Irony attributed to the expat's mindset, not the narrator's; shifts to his internal voice mid-paragraph and must not be flattened.

proposed.en: we're all respectable people here, after all
proposed.zh: 我们这儿可都是体面人
proposed.ja: ここにいるのはみな常識人のはずだ

terms.gloss: Squirming/fidgeting in his chair — the expat's discomfort as he repeats himself.
terms.why_hard: Small physical beat; wrong register ('wriggling') reads comic rather than uneasy.

proposed.ja: 椅子の上で落ち着かず身じろぎしながら

terms.gloss: 'Rolling out this service' — Russian tech-biz calque of внедрить (deploy/launch).
terms.why_hard: 'Внедрять' has no single English match; 'introduce/implement' reads bureaucratic instead of product-speak.

proposed.zh: 我们正在上线这项服务
proposed.ja: このサービスを展開している

terms.gloss: Selection competition for the Potanin Scholarship (Vladimir Potanin's foundation), a prestigious student fellowship in Russia
terms.why_hard: Requires knowing this is a merit-based scholarship contest with public speaking/debate rounds, not a generic 'selection'

proposed.ja: ポターニン奨学生選抜

terms.gloss: Classmate/acquaintance of Durov quoted as source
terms.why_hard: Proper name transliteration must stay consistent across mentions

terms.gloss: Epithet for Durov as an 'internet totem/idol' figure among peers
terms.why_hard: Metaphor tying Durov to reverence/idol status must be rendered consistently with later 'небожитель' epithet

proposed.ja: インターネットの守護神的存在

terms.gloss: Epithet: 'the troll from the front desk', describing young Durov's classroom persona
terms.why_hard: Requires knowing 'troll' internet slang connotation predates its later toxic sense; front desk implies attentive/provocative student

terms.gloss: 'Celestial being/dweller of Olympus' - epithet for Durov's elevated, remote status
terms.why_hard: Must contrast with 'спускается в народ' (descending to the people) - religious/mythological register needs preserving

terms.gloss: United Russia, the ruling political party
terms.why_hard: Must use official party name consistently, not descriptive paraphrase

terms.gloss: Military department/chair at university providing reserve officer training
terms.why_hard: Soviet/Russian-specific institution with no direct Western equivalent; must not be confused with ROTC exactly

terms.gloss: Platoon commander (student cadet rank within military training)
terms.why_hard: Military rank abbreviation; needs consistent rendering across mentions of the anecdote

terms.gloss: Academic Council of the university, faculty governing body
terms.why_hard: Formal institutional term, must not be rendered as generic 'meeting'

terms.gloss: Student activist body/council involved in institutional/PR activities
terms.why_hard: Soviet-era term for student activist cadre, connotes semi-official student leadership

terms.gloss: 'Military cunning/stratagem' - phrase used to justify cheating on exams as tactically acceptable
terms.why_hard: Idiomatic justification with ironic tone; literal translation risks losing the wry humor

terms.gloss: Philologist/student of philology - Durov's academic specialization
terms.why_hard: Russian 'филология' covers language & literature studies broadly; must be consistent with earlier segments' rendering of his major

terms.gloss: stop showing off / acting arrogant / posturing
terms.why_hard: Colloquial and rude; mistranslating as simply 'don't make trouble' loses the swaggering nuance.

terms.gloss: the female exam proctor / monitor (pejoratively likened to a prison overseer)
terms.why_hard: Durov's perspective reduces an academic proctor to a prison warden; translating literally as 'overseer' can sound strange.

terms.gloss: insecure bitch / uptight cow (crude gendered put-down)
terms.why_hard: Literally 'complex-ridden goat'; needs a natural sounding idiomatic insult in the target register.

proposed.ja: コンプレックスまみれの女狐

terms.gloss: the ship has sailed / too late to change anything
terms.why_hard: Standard Russian idiom that should not be translated literally as a train departing.

terms.gloss: the dean's office / university faculty administration
terms.why_hard: A fundamental administrative unit in Russian universities that doesn't map 1:1 to Anglo-American departments.

terms.gloss: slapped them with failing grades ('unsatisfactory')
terms.why_hard: 'Неуд' is Soviet/Russian academic slang for 'неудовлетворительно' (F/failing grade), and 'влепили' is colloquial violence.

terms.gloss: sounded people out / put out feelers on the university forum
terms.why_hard: Idiom 'забросить удочки' (cast fishing lines) combined with mid-2000s university forum culture (spbgu.ru).

proposed.en: put out feelers on the forum
proposed.ja: フォーラムに探りを入れた

terms.gloss: dunces/dimwits from the tuition-paying (commercial) department
terms.why_hard: Russian universities had free state-funded merit spots vs. lower-standard paid spots; 'платное отделение' implies rich, unacademic students.

proposed.ja: 有料コースの能無し学生たち

terms.gloss: the mobsters / the pair of conspirators (Durov and Perekopsky acting in cartel-like solidarity)
terms.why_hard: Humorous/ironic hyperbole used by the narrator to describe Durov and Perekopsky.

proposed.ja: マフィア気取りの二人は

terms.gloss: the academic department / chair
terms.why_hard: A Russian university sub-division within a faculty (факультет); distinct from деканат.

terms.gloss: he said, she said / conflicting testimony where neither side backs down
terms.why_hard: Poetic/rhetorical idiom for an irreconcilable verbal deadlock.

proposed.en: it came down to word against word

terms.gloss: head of the academic department (Pavel's father, Valery Durov, head of Classical Philology)
terms.why_hard: Crucial context: Valery Durov was head of the Department of Classical Philology at SPbSU, giving Pavel leverage.

terms.gloss: backed down / gave ground / retreated
terms.why_hard: Colloquial/driver slang applied to institutional retreat under political pressure.

terms.gloss: formal severe reprimand (official disciplinary measure in Russian administrative culture)
terms.why_hard: Official bureaucratic penalty in Russian institutions with specific legal/HR weight.

terms.gloss: Sergei Bogdanov, Dean of the Faculty of Philology at St Petersburg State University
terms.why_hard: Real historical figure; translators should recognize his identity and role at SPbSU.

terms.gloss: a boor, insolent cad, lout lacking basic respect
terms.why_hard: 'Хам' / 'хамство' is a deeply Russian moral-cultural category of aggressive insolence, stronger than just 'rude person'.

terms.gloss: a folding triptych / polyptych icon board
terms.why_hard: Traditional Orthodox religious art term (folding icon panels) applied here eccentrically to a giant wall collage.

proposed.ja: 折り畳み式多翼祭壇画

terms.gloss: gesso / chalk priming used in traditional Russian icon painting
terms.why_hard: Specialist Orthodox iconographic term for alabaster/chalk primer spread on canvas/wood; vital to preserve the bizarre religious-art vibe.

proposed.zh: 胶矾底子（象牙石膏粉底）
proposed.ja: レフカス（イコン用下地）

terms.gloss: faces/visages of Orthodox saints (liturgical register)
terms.why_hard: 'Лик' is the sacred, ecclesiastical register for 'face' in Russian icon art, contrasting with 'лица' or 'фотографии'.

terms.gloss: a solid half-hour / for a relentless thirty minutes
terms.why_hard: Colloquial emphatic time marker; implies endurance of tediousness.

terms.gloss: the precursor / prototype of VKontakte
terms.why_hard: Reflects the dean's eccentric claim of having invented social networking analogously.

terms.gloss: The 'Mafia' group — an influential circle of forum users/moderators around Durov on spbgu.ru, not the game.
terms.why_hard: Could be misread as the party game 'Mafia' popular in Russia; it is a named clique of the forum's inner circle.

terms.gloss: Catchy plea: 'Pasha, sell the forum and buy yourself a car!' — a joke embodying the sell-out temptation.
terms.why_hard: It frames the whole scene as a temptation narrative; the rhyme/rhythm in Russian ('форум/машину') is hard, but sense must stay literal.

proposed.en: 'Pasha, sell the forum — buy yourself a car!'
proposed.ja: 「パーシャ、フォーラムを売って車でも買えよ！」

terms.gloss: Diminutive of Pavel (Durov), signaling friendly intimacy.
terms.why_hard: Languages without productive diminutives lose the informality; a consistent handling of 'Pasha/Pavel' is needed book-wide.

terms.gloss: Elnara — female forum member, first name only in the original.
terms.why_hard: Gender is not obvious from the name to non-Russian readers; keep first-name-only as the source does.

terms.gloss: A 'media Virgil' — someone guiding Durov through the world of press and publicity, as Virgil guided Dante.
terms.why_hard: The Dante's-Inferno allusion must survive; 'media-savvy guide' flattens it.

proposed.zh: 媒体界的“维吉尔”（引路人之意）
proposed.ja: メディア界のウェルギリウス

terms.term: «Не хочу машину, – отмахивался Дуров. – Меня укачивает»
terms.gloss: 'I don't want a car — I get carsick,' a deadpan deflection hiding his real refusal to sell out.
terms.why_hard: 'укачивает' (motion sickness) is a wry understatement; must stay flippant, not literal-medical.

proposed.en: 'I don't want a car — I get carsick,' Durov waved it off.
proposed.zh: “我不想要车，”杜罗夫摆摆手，“我晕车。”
proposed.ja: 「車なんていらない。車酔いするんだ」とドゥロフは取り合わなかった。

terms.gloss: Forum moderator — a role with specific 2000s internet-culture weight in Russian forums.
terms.why_hard: Not 'editor' or 'administrator'; the term should be uniform across the book's forum scenes.

terms.gloss: Faculty of International Relations at St Petersburg State University, where spbgu.ru and its community originated.

proposed.ja: 自動車化時代の申し子

terms.gloss: The disused airfield where Durov had previously gone to sit and read.

terms.gloss: Consumer society, personified here as the force replacing open space with shopping centers.

terms.gloss: Huge shopping malls likened to decadent, overweening Babylonian structures.

proposed.ja: バビロンさながらの巨大モール

terms.gloss: The minibus driver characterized as a large, intimidating bruiser.

terms.gloss: A stock minibus demand asking which passenger has not passed their fare forward to the driver.

proposed.ja: まだ運賃を回していないのは誰だ？

terms.gloss: Colloquial abbreviation for the university's Faculty of Economics.

terms.gloss: The elected or designated student who organizes and represents a university class group.

terms.gloss: The staffed university cloakroom where students check coats on entering the building.

terms.gloss: Web-industry language for a flow of users or visitors, applied metaphorically to students moving through the hall.

terms.gloss: A crowd of real people viewed as potential users and social-network traffic.

terms.gloss: Forming social connections in offline life, presented as the problem a social network could solve.

proposed.ja: 小さなケースを提げた男

terms.gloss: The two elite parallel first-year streams (class 1 and class 2) in a Russian school numbering system

proposed.en: autistic kid in glasses with a huge minus prescription

terms.gloss: Lake Zerkalnoye (Mirror Lake), a Leningrad-oblast camp lake used by 239

terms.gloss: Two courtyards by the school nicknamed Smoke-1 and Smoke-2, hangouts for smoking and fights

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, the future founder of VKontakte.

terms.gloss: Durov’s surname-based website used to share university study materials.

terms.why_hard: The Soviet-era word is the whole point; non-Russian readers (and especially zh/ja readers) have no native anchor, so it needs a functional equivalent or brief in-text gloss.

terms.gloss: Soviet-flavored bureaucratic phrase 'broad strata of the population' used semi-ironically for market capture by a product.

proposed.zh: 不是团队型选手，而是想征服世界的“蝎子”型人物

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, founder of VKontakte and later Telegram

terms.gloss: Yuri Milner, Russian-Israeli tech investor, DST Global founder

terms.gloss: Dmitry Grishin, then-CEO of Mail.ru Group

terms.gloss: Vlad Tsyplukhin, VKontakte press secretary hired by Durov

terms.gloss: Likely a Game Insight executive or contact; surname only in text

terms.gloss: Game developers/industry people; informal collective for those in the gaming business

terms.gloss: Monetization; the revenue-sharing mechanism for apps on VKontakte's platform

proposed.ja: グリシンのプラットフォーム

terms.gloss: Military action; metaphor for corporate conflict between VKontakte and Mail.ru

terms.gloss: Peacemaking, reconciliation; archaic/formal word for ending a conflict

terms.gloss: VKontakte's advertising system/self-serve ad platform

terms.gloss: Pavel Durov, VKontakte founder
terms.why_hard: Must stay surname-only or full name consistently with the rest of the book

terms.gloss: Book epithet for Durov as the company’s sacred figurehead

terms.gloss: VK co-founders (Mirilashvili, Leviev et al.), not Durov alone

terms.gloss: VKontakte social network

terms.gloss: intellectual property (copyrighted music, video, etc.)

terms.gloss: copyright holders / rights-holders (labels, studios)

terms.gloss: A cramped closet-like room where the programmers are clustered.
